slides.title: Introduction CAN
slides.body:
The CAN (Controller Area Network) bus is broadcast digital bus designed to operate at speeds
from 20kb/s to 1Mb/s. The transmission rate depends on the bus length and transceiver
speed.
The CAN network protocol has been defined to provide deterministic communication
in complex distributed systems with the following features/capabilities:
- Possibility of assigning priority to messages and guaranteed maximum latency times.
- Multicast communication with bit-oriented synchronization.
- System wide data consistency.
- Multimaster access to the bus.
- Error detection and signalling with automatic retransmission of corrupted messages.
- Detection of possible permanent failures of nodes and automatic switching off of
defective nodes.
IntroductionCAN -

slides.title: Network Topology CAN
slides.body:
- The interface between a CAN controller chip and a two-wire differential bus typically
consists of a transmitting and a receiving amplifier (transceiver = transmit and receive).
- The transceiver must convert the electrical representation of a bit from the one in use by
the controller to the one defined for the bus.
- In addition, it must provide sufficient output current to drive the bus electrical state, and
protect the controller chip against overloading.
- As a receiver, the CAN transceiver provides the recessive signal level and protects the
controller chip input comparator against excessive voltages on the bus lines.
- Furthermore, it detects bus errors such as line breakage, short circuits, shorts to ground,
etc.
- A further function of the transceiver can also be the galvanic isolation between a CAN node
and the bus line.
CAN -

slides.title: Transmission rate & Bus lenght CAN
slides.body:
- Because of the definition of the bit time, it clearly exists a
dependency between the bit time and the signal
propagation delay, that is, between the maximum achievable
bit rate (or transmission speed) and the length of the bus
- The signal propagation delay to be considered for the
computation of the maximum allowed bus length includes
several stages
- For short, high speed networks, the biggest limitation to bus
length is the transceivers propagation delay.
Transmission rate & Bus lenghtCAN -

slides.title: Bus termination CAN
slides.body:
Electrical signals on the bus are reflected at the
ends of the electrical line unless measures are
taken. For the node to read the bus level correctly it
is important that signal reflections are avoided. This
is done by terminating the bus line with a
termination resistor at both ends of the bus and by
avoiding unnecessarily long stubs lines of the bus
- For high speed CAN, ISO 11898 requires a cable
with a nominal impedance of 120 ohms, and
therefore 120 ohm resistors should be used for
termination (only the devices on the ends of the
cable need termination resistors).
- For Low-Speed CAN, each device on the network
needs a termination resistor for each data line.
Bus terminationCAN -

slides.title: Physical encoding of Dominant and recessive states CAN
slides.body:
- CAN specifies two logical states:
recessive and dominant. According
to ISO-11898-2, a differential voltage
is used to represent recessive and
dominant states.
- In the recessive state (usually logic
1), the differential voltage on CAN H
and CAN L is less than the minimum
threshold (<0.5V receiver input or
<1.5V transmitter output). In the
dominant state (logic 0), the
differential voltage on CAN H and
CAN L is greater than the minimum
threshold.
Physical encoding of Dominant and recessive statesCAN -

slides.title: Message Format CAN
slides.body:
In CAN, there are 4 different types of frames, according to their content and function:
- DAT A FRAMEs contain data information from a source to possibly multiple receivers.
- REMOTE FRAMEs are used to request transmission of a corresponding (with the same identifier)
DATA FRAME.
- ERROR FRAMEs are transmitted whenever a node on the network detects an error.
- OVERLOAD FRAMEs are used fro flow control, to request an additional time delay before the
transmission of a DATA or REMOTE frame.
Message FormatCAN -

slides.title: Data frame CAN
Data frame (Identifier) CAN
slides.body:
The CAN protocol requires that all contending
messages have a unique identifier. The identifier
field consists of 11 (+1) bits in standard format
and 29 (+3) bits in extended format.
The field is built:
- the first 11 bits of the identifier;
- RTR (Remote Transmission Request) bit in the
standard and extended format;
- SRR (Substitute Remote Request), only in
extended format; it’s only a place holder
- Single IDE bit (Identifier Extension, always
recessive)
- the remaining 18 least significant identifier
bits
Data frame (Identifier)CAN -

slides.title: Data frame (Control, Data and Interframe space) CAN
slides.body:
The control field contains 6 bits. The first two bits are
reserved or predefined in content.
The following four bits define the length of the data
content (Data Length Content, or DLC) in bytes. If the
dominant bit is interpreted as 1 (contrary to the
common notation in which it is read as 0) and the
recessive as 0, the four DLC bits are the unsigned binary
coding of the length.
The data field position is on the right side of the control
field. The maximum dimension of the data field is 8
bytes.
Data frames and remote frames are separated by an
INTERFRAME space (7 recessive bits) on the bus.
Data frame (Control, Data and Interframe space)CAN -

slides.title: Remote/Error/Overload frame CAN
slides.body:
A remote frame is used to request the transmission of a message with a given identifier from a
remote node. A remote frame has the same format of a data frame with the following
characteristics:
- the identifier field is used to indicate the identifier of the requested message
- the data field is always empty (0 bytes)
- the DLC field indicates the data length of the requested message (not the transmitted one)
- the RTR bit in the arbitration field is always set to recessive
The error frame is not a true frame, but rather the result of an error signalling and recovery. The
details of such an event are described in the following sections.
The ERROR FRAME and the OVERLOAD FRAME are of fixed form as well and not
coded by the method of bit stuffing
Remote/Error/Overload frameCAN -

slides.title: Error management CAN
slides.body:
The CAN protocol is designed for safe data transfers and provides mechanisms for error
detection, signalling and self-diagnostics, including measures for fault confinement, which
prevent faulty nodes from affecting the status of the network.
The general measures for error detection are based on the capability of each node of monitoring
broadcast transmissions over the bus, whether it is a transmitter or a receiver, and to signal error
conditions resulting from several sources. Corrupted messages are flagged by any node detecting
an error. Such messages are aborted and will be retransmitted automatically.
The protocol requires that receivers acknowledge reception of the message by changing the
content of the ACK FIELD. The ACK FIELD is two bits long and contains the ACK SLOT and the ACK
DELIMITER. In the ACK FIELD the transmitting station sends two recessive bits. All receiver
nodes that detect a correct message (after CRC checks), inform the sender by changing the
recessive bit of the ACK SLOT into a dominant bit.
Error managementCAN -

slides.title: CRC checks CAN
slides.body:
The CRC portion of the frame is obtained by selecting the input polynomial (to be divided)
as the stream of bits from the START OF FRAME bit (included) to the DATA FIELD (if
present) followed by 15 zeros.
This polynomial is divided by the generator:
The remainder of the division is the CRC SEQUENCE portion of the frame
CRC checksCAN -

slides.title: Error types CAN
slides.body:
There are 5 different error types:
- BIT ERROR: a unit that is sending a bit on the bus also monitors the bus. A BIT ERROR has to be detected at
that bit time, when the bit value that is monitored is different from the bit value that is sent. Exceptions are
the recessive bits sent as part of the arbitration process or the ACK SLOT .
- STUFF ERROR: a STUFF ERROR is detected at the 6th consecutive occurrence of the same bit in a message
field that is subject to stuffing.
- CRC ERROR: if the CRC computed by the receiver differs from the one stored in the message frame.
- FORM ERROR: when a fixed-form bit field contains one or more illegal bits. (Note, that for a Receiver a
dominant bit during the last bit of END OR FRAME is not treated as FORM ERROR, this is the possible cause
of inconsistent message omission and duplicates).
- ACKNOWLEDGMENT ERROR: detected by a transmitter if a recessive bit is found on the ACK SLOT .
Error typesCAN -

slides.title: Error Confinement Mechanisms CAN
slides.body:
Each node on netwoek has two error counters: the Transmit Error Counter and the Receive Error Counter.
There are several rules governing how these counters are incremented and/or decremented.
A transmitter detecting a fault increments its Transmit Error Counter +8 for each corrupted message, and
decrements it of 1 for each correctly send message.
o A node starts out in Error Active mode. When any one of the two Error Counters raises above 127, the node will
enter a state known as Error Passive and when the Transmit Error Counter raises above 255, the node will enter
the Bus Off state.
o An Error Active node will transmit Active Error Flags when it detects errors.
o An Error Passive node will transmit Passive Error Flags when it detects errors.
o A node which is Bus Off will not transmit anything on the bus at all.
Error Confinement MechanismsCAN -

slides.title: Network Specification DBC CAN
slides.body:
The Network specification, that is used to decode raw messages on CAN, into physical values and signals, is the
DBC File – Data Base Can
Each CAN network has a dedicated DBC file.
In the DBC file are listed all the ECUs present on Network, and all the received and transmitted messages.
For each message is specified the transmission methode (cyclic, on event..), the DLC, the identification of the
message, the cycle time and the signals included in the message.

slides.title: Common CAN type CAN
slides.body:
The main CAN bus that are used on the vehicle are classified
on the basis of the baud rate.
The most used network are:
- C-CAN: the baud rate is 500 kb/s;
- B-CAN: the baud rate is 50 kb/s;
- BH-CAN: the baud rate is 125 kb/s;
- FD-CAN: the baud rate is variable up to 15Mb/s.
Usually on the C-CAN there are for sure all the ECUs that are
emission relevant in accord to EOBD normative.
Usually on the BH-CAN there are all the ECUs that manage
multimedial information

slides.title: Access to CAN bus CAN
Local Interconnect Network LIN
slides.body:
Local Interconnect Network LIN -
LIN (Local Interconnect Network) is a serial network
protocol used for communication between components in
vehicles.
It is used typically for nodes that do not need excessive
bandwidth, performance, or extreme safety requirements.
LIN is a broadcast serial network, comprising one master
and typically up to 16 slaves.
All messages are initiated by the master with at most one
slave replying to a given message identifier.
LIN Network is mainly used for smart actuators and
sensors, that need to transmit/receive less information
with less frequency.

slides.title: Differences and integration with CAN Network LIN
slides.body:
LIN provides low cost efficient communication in applications where
the bandwidth and versatility of CAN are not required.
Typically, it is used for sub-systems that are not critical to vehicle
performance or safety.
- Lin Network is easier to realize and cheaper than CAN Netwok
because it has only one wire vs. double wire of CAN Network.
It is also easier to configure, and to implement additional extensions.
Since there is one master of the network, no collision strategies are needed.
- Can network is more robust to disturbance and reaches higher speed than LIN Network
The LIN master has also a CAN connection, and performs gateway functions.
Differences and integration with CAN NetworkLIN -

slides.title: Protocol main features LIN
slides.body:
- Single master, up to 16 slaves
- Slave Node Position Detection (SNPD) allows node address assignment after power-up
- Single wire communications up to 19.2 kbit/s for 40 meter bus length.
- Guaranteed latency times.
- Variable length of data frame (2, 4 and 8 byte).
- Data checksum and error detection.
- Detection of defective nodes.
- Operating voltage of 12 V
- Standard compliant: ISO 9141
Protocol main featuresLIN -

slides.title: Hardware features and physical layer LIN
slides.body:
LIN Bus is connected to the
12V power supply with a pull up
Resistance 1 kΩ in the master node,
and typically 30 kΩ in a slave node.
Series diodes are connected to
avoid overvoltage.
The connection to the ground
Can also be on vehicle chassis.
The bus operates with two complementary logic levels:The dominant value with a voltage close to
ground represents a logical 0.
The recessive value with an electrical voltage close to the battery voltage, and represent a logical 1

slides.title: Master and Slaves LIN
slides.body:
Master and SlavesLIN -
The Master has the complete control of both the bus, on which the data
are entered, and the communication protocol.
Determines when to initiate message transfer to all slave nodes.
It determines when to start message transfer on the bus, send the Synch Break (predefined sequence of
bytes preceding a frame) and receives wake up Break bits from Slaves when they request to communicate.
Performs the monitoring of the data and check byte, verifying their consistency and correctness
respectively.
The Slave is one of the nodes present on the bus that can receive or transmit data when the Master decide
it. It synchronizes on the Synch Byte issued by the Master, analyze the identifier-field bits and based on
the content of the identifier field, determines what to do.

slides.title: Message frames LIN
slides.body:
Data is transferred across the bus in fixed form messages of selectable lengths. The master transmits a message
header, that consists of fields, that synchronize and identify it. The slaves respond with a data frame that
consists of data and checksum.
- Message Header 🡪 it consists of a break, used to identify the start of frame, a sync field, used by the slave
node for clock synchronization, and the identifier that denotes a specific message address, but not the
destination.
- Message Response 🡪 upon the rception of the ID, the polled slave begins the message response which
consists of 1 to 8 bytes of data, and 8-bit checksum.
Message framesLIN -

slides.title: Message frames LIN
slides.body:
Upon receiving the header, each slave checks the ID to determine what it needs to publish or subscribe.
If the slave task needs to publish a response, it transmits one to eight data bytes to the bus followed by a
checksum byte.
Message framesLIN -
The master controls the sequencing of message frames, which is defined in a schedule that can be changed as
needed. The Master uses one or more predefined scheduling tables to start the sending and receiving on the
LIN bus. These scheduling tables contain relative timing, where the message sending is initiated.

slides.title: Scheduling Tables LIN
slides.body:
Scheduling TablesLIN -
A key property of the LIN protocol is the use of schedule tables.
Schedule tables make it possible to assure that the bus will never be overloaded and to guarantee the
periodicity of signals.
The schedule table in the LDF defines the sequence and time grid in which messages are sent. Once
the table has been worked through, the Master begins with the first message again.
It’s possible that several schedule tables co-exist in a LIN. When a schedule table has been performed,
any one of the rest of schedule tables may be performed. It depends on system policies.
The idea to support different type of schedule is that there is always a set of schedule that runs
continuously, in normal operation, but if there is a specific situation or request, another schedule can
be started.

slides.title: Network Specifications: LDF LIN
slides.body:
Network Specifications: LDFLIN -
The configuration of the LIN network is described in the LIN Description File LDF .
In the LDF all LIN messages with correspondent signals are described, and it contains also features of the
network, such as the number of nodes present, and in which schedule the messages appears, with also
their periodicity.
For example, it defines the baud rate, the ordering and time delays for the master task’s transmission of
headers, and the behavior of each slave task in response.
Each LIN present, has a dedicated LDF File.

slides.title: Frames types LIN
slides.body:
Frames typesLIN -
- Unconditional frame 🡪 This is the normal type of LIN communication. The Master
sends a frame header in a scheduled frame slot and the designated Slave node fills the
frame with data. Unconditional frames carry signals and their frame identifiers are in
the range 0 (0x00) to 59 (0x3B).
- Event-triggered frame 🡪 The purpose of this is to increase the responsiveness of the
LIN cluster without assigning too much of the bus bandwidth to the polling of multiple
slave nodes. The first data byte of the carried unconditional frame shall be equal to a
protected identifier assigned to an event-triggered frame. A slave shall reply with an
associated unconditional frame only if its data value has changed. If none of the slave
tasks responds to the header the rest of the frame slot is silent and the header is
ignored. If more than one slave task responds to the header in the same frame slot a
collision will occur, and the master has to resolve the collision by requesting all
associated unconditional frames before requesting the event-triggered frame again.

slides.title: Frames types LIN
slides.body:
Frames typesLIN -
Unconditional Frame example

slides.title: Frames types LIN
slides.body:
Frames typesLIN -
- Sporadic frame🡪 Sent by Master only when it is known that a Slave has updated information to publish.
The header of a sporadic frame shall only be sent in its associated frame slot when the master knows
that a signal carried in the frame has been updated. The publisher of the sporadic frame shall always
provide the response to the header.
- Diagnostic frame🡪 These always carry diagnostic or configuration data and they always contain eight
data bytes. The identifier is either 0x3C, called master request frame, or 0x3D, called slave response
frame. Before generating the header of a diagnostic frame, the master asks its diagnostic module if it
shall be sent or if the bus shall be silent. The slave publish and subscribe to the response according to
their diagnostic module.
- User-defined frame🡪 These can carry any kind of information. Their identifier is 62 (0x3E). The header
of a user-defined frame is always transmitted when a frame slot allocated to the frame is processed

slides.title: Sleep and WakeUp LIN
slides.body:
Sleep and WakeUpLIN -
LIN network has a mechanism that allows devices to enter the sleep mode and so conserve power.
All slaves may be forced into sleep mode by the master sending a diagnostic master request frame with the
first data byte equal to zero.
This special frame is called the go-to-sleep command.
Slaves also automatically enter sleep mode if the LIN is inactive for more than four seconds.
LIN also has a mechanism for waking devices on the bus.
Wakeup is one task that may be initiated by any node on the bus (a slave as well as the master).
Each slave should detect the wakeup request and be ready to process headers within 100 ms.
The master should also detect the wakeup request and start sending headers when the slave nodes are
ready (within 100 ms to 150 ms after receiving the wakeup request).
If the master does not issue headers within 150 ms after receiving the first wakeup request, then the slave
shall try again up to 4 times, before to detect an error.
